description: Flame Frontier is an evidence dashboard for NASA’s microgravity combustion data. It maps every space fire test we could trace, from the PSI database and NASA papers, against the air future Moon-base crews will breathe, and shows where the evidence runs out: only 2 solid-material burns in Moon-base air, none in partial gravity. Every number links to its source. Built in Python and JavaScript, with a cited AI Q&A.
summary:
Flame Frontier is an interactive, AI-assisted web dashboard that maps NASA’s microgravity combustion evidence against the air future crews will breathe. NASA expects Moon bases and pressurized rovers to run at 30% oxygen or more at reduced pressure, which makes materials more flammable, yet the relevant data is spread across 24 PSI investigations and about 12 TB of files.

We parsed PSI test tables, metadata and NASA reports into one traceable dataset, then placed every solid-material test by its oxygen and pressure. The finding: of 134 solid-material tests in our sources, only 2 burned in Moon-base air, both at one airflow, and none in partial gravity.

The dashboard addresses all three challenge goals. It ranks the 24 investigations for each habitat using visible rules, exports 586 sourced tests for flammability modelling, and maps prevention, detection and suppression research against habitat gaps. A cited Q&A answers only from NASA passages, with code-checked citations.

Every number links to its NASA source, and a Known Limits page states what the data cannot show. The result is a clear map of where NASA’s fire evidence ends, so the next experiment knows where to start.
details:
What it does

Flame Frontier is an interactive web dashboard that answers one question for NASA’s next missions: how much fire-safety evidence exists for the air future crews will breathe? NASA expects Moon bases and pressurized rovers to use 30% oxygen or more at reduced pressure (10.2 psi or less), which makes materials more flammable. The relevant experiments are spread across 24 combustion investigations and about 12 TB in NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) database.

How it works

We downloaded PSI test tables, investigation metadata, NASA reports and papers, and built a reproducible Python pipeline. It cleans the tables, classifies each test (material, sample shape, oxygen, pressure, airflow, outcome) and attaches a source to every value: a file and row, or a report page. Ambiguous crew notes were reviewed by hand, never guessed.

The site then tells the story visually:

  • Story: 134 solid-material space fire tests appear as dots and sort by the air they burned in. 104 match no crew habitat, 28 match the ISS cabin, only 2 match Moon-base air, and none were done in partial gravity.
  • Evidence: an oxygen-versus-pressure map with the Moon-base zone and what’s missing inside it, plus NASA’s published BASS-II flammability boundary with the flight tests we could rebuild from public files.
  • Explore: all 24 investigations ranked for each habitat with visible scoring rules, side-by-side comparison, a habitat gap grid, and prevention, detection and suppression research mapped against those gaps.
  • Ask: questions in plain English, answered by AI only from 246 cited NASA passages, with code checking every citation and number.
  • Flame Sandbox and Clips: a labelled teaching model of Earth versus microgravity flames, and real NASA flight video.

Benefits and intended impact

Engineers choosing materials and suppression systems can see exactly which conditions have evidence and which don’t. Researchers can download 586 sourced tests for their own flammability models, and the gap grid works as a to-do list for future experiments such as LUCI and FM2. When NASA publishes new data, the same pipeline can add it.

Tools

Python (pandas, pydantic, openpyxl), JavaScript with Vite, Apache ECharts, Three.js, a keyword search index (BM25), the Anthropic Claude API, Vercel hosting with a small Python function, GitHub, Playwright for visual checks, and gitleaks for secret scanning. The project was built with help from Claude and Claude Code. No special hardware.

What makes it creative

Instead of a generic dashboard, it frames the data as a single question with a striking answer: two tests. It checks “whose oxygen?” in every dataset, separating the air around a flame from a burner’s oxygen stream so values aren’t misread. It openly reports that only 7 of NASA’s roughly 50 published boundary points can be rebuilt from public files. And it turns missing evidence into a navigable map of what to test next.

Factors we considered

  • Accuracy and trust: every number traces to its source, AI never produces a chart value, and a Known Limits page states what the data cannot show.
  • Two audiences: plain-language explanations for the public, with full technical detail for scientists.
  • Durability: the site keeps working without a live AI key, so judges can use it for months.
  • Responsible use: open data only, copyrighted text kept out, secrets scanned before every push, accessibility and mobile support, and AI costs of a few cents.
